name: TMEM165-CDG (CDG-IIk)
aliases: congenital disorder of glycosylation type IIk

reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: A type II CDG caused by defects in TMEM165, a Golgi transporter involved in manganese and calcium homeostasis required for glycosyltransferase activity
Distinguished by a prominent skeletal phenotype with spondylo-epi-metaphyseal dysplasia, short stature and skeletal dysplasia in addition to developmental delay
Hepatic involvement, growth failure and variable dysmorphism accompany the skeletal features
Transferrin analysis shows a type II pattern reflecting defective galactosylation of complex glycan antennae
Because the defect involves Golgi manganese handling, in vitro and some clinical data suggest galactose or manganese supplementation can improve glycosylation markers
Management is supportive and multidisciplinary; galactose supplementation may be trialled with biochemical monitoring
Diagnosis is confirmed by TMEM165 molecular genetic testing
reference.pathophysiology: TMEM165 is a Golgi membrane protein that regulates manganese and calcium homeostasis in the secretory pathway. Many Golgi glycosyltransferases, particularly galactosyltransferases, depend on manganese as a cofactor, so loss of TMEM165 function impairs terminal galactosylation of complex N-glycans, producing a type II processing defect on transferrin analysis. The manganese dependence explains why supplying galactose or manganese can partially restore glycosylation. Hypoglycosylation of bone matrix and other proteins is thought to drive the characteristic skeletal dysplasia.
additionalDifferentials: Other type II CDG subtypes (e.g. MGAT2-CDG, B4GALT1-CDG, COG-complex CDG, SLC35A2-CDG)
Primary skeletal dysplasias and spondylo-epi-metaphyseal dysplasias
Mucopolysaccharidoses and other storage disorders with bone involvement
Type I CDGs when the transferrin pattern is ambiguous
Hepatic involvement from other metabolic causes
additionalInvestigations: Transferrin isoelectric focusing or mass spectrometry showing a type II pattern
Biochemical monitoring during a galactose supplementation trial
redFlags: Progressive skeletal deformity or severe short stature
Failure to thrive with multisystem involvement
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is variable; the skeletal dysplasia and growth failure are often prominent, and biochemical improvement with galactose supplementation has been reported, although its long-term clinical benefit is still being defined. Neurodevelopmental outcome depends on disease severity.
pitfalls: Investigating the skeletal dysplasia in isolation without considering a glycosylation disorder
Not distinguishing type I from type II defects on transferrin analysis
Overlooking a potential galactose or manganese-responsive component
Interpreting biochemical response as proven clinical cure
references: Scriver's OMMBID, congenital disorders of glycosylation
Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics, disorders of glycosylation
management: Trial oral galactose supplementation, given the Golgi manganese dependence of galactosylation, and monitor transferrin glycosylation markers and clinical response during the trial
Provide multidisciplinary supportive care directed at the skeletal, hepatic and developmental manifestations
Manage the spondylo-epi-metaphyseal dysplasia and short stature with orthopaedic input and physiotherapy
Monitor liver function and imaging for hepatic involvement
Assess growth, endocrine status and development, providing developmental support as needed
Offer genetic counselling and family screening, as the disorder is inherited
